name: Cossack
lede: Cossack is a dark yellowish green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, apparently borrowed from the name for the horsemen of the Eurasian steppe, though the dictionary gives no reason for the pairing.

sections.title: A borrowed name, unexplained
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul list Cossack at #2F512A on plate 38, row K, column 2 of their 1930 dictionary, dating its first recorded use to 1892, decades before the dictionary itself [1]. The ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 files the swatch as "grayish green" [1]. Why a dark green took the name of the Cossacks, horsemen historically associated with the Russian and Ukrainian steppe, is undocumented in the 29 books behind our concordance; dark greens were a common dye color for military and riding coats, but no source we checked ties this swatch to that practice [1].

In our color graph the nearest named neighbor is [[meadowgrass|Meadowgrass]], 3.6 units away [1]. A little further, at 6.3 units, is [[hunter-green|Hunter green]], a fellow dark green with a similarly outdoor name [1]. The Munsell notation is 8.8GY 3.1/4.9, and the swatch sits with our [[green|green]] family, close enough to the yellow modifier in its ISCC name to also sit near [[yellow|yellow]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 0.61% of 23,781 paintings, 146 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 61 [2]. That is more common than 52% of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1800s, present in 0.6% of the 8,345 paintings from that century, twice the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as a shadow, in 51% of its 61 appearances [2]. Camille Pissarro is its most devoted painter, holding it in 4 of 50 works here, 5.3 times the baseline of the museums his paintings come from [2]. The earliest match dates to 1530, by Girolamo da Carpi, 400 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
